ann_33.text: Through this part, non-anginal chest pain (about 7%), atypical angina (about 20%) and typical angina (about 21%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 31%).

More vessels coloured and higher cholesterol raise it steadily, from about 31% at 0 vessels to about 90% at 2 (flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher) and from about 18% at 193 mg/dL to about 55% at 308 mg/dL; a flat ST segment raises it to about 55%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 38% (on the training data only).
Being a woman and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL each lower it to about 5%, and older age lowers it here steadily, from about 37% at 42 to about 27% at 66 years (on the training data only).

A downsloping ST segment and maximum heart rate change it only slightly here; by shape: maximum heart rate steadily (on the training data only; the model has little data on the downsloping ST segment, 17 patients).

ann_34.text: This part acts on 93 of 242 training patients (38%); 76 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, chest pain brought on by exercise, a resting blood pressure of 140 mm Hg, 1 vessel coloured, 1.8 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it clearly raises the predicted risk from about 89% to above 99%.
Through it, typical angina lowers that patient's predicted risk from above 99% to about 89% (on the training data only).
More ST depression clearly raises the predicted risk in an uneven way, and even more so with a reversible thallium defect (from about 31% to about 74%, against no change otherwise).

For patients with a downsloping ST segment, ST depression adds to the predicted risk through this part with nothing until about 1.9 mm, then steadily, for most patients, but for patients with non-anginal chest pain and patients whose chest pain is brought on by exercise it rises slowly at first, then faster (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 10% to about 66%; on the training data only; the model has little data on this).

A reversible thallium defect, higher resting blood pressure, an ST segment that is not upsloping, more ST depression, chest pain on exercise and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL each raise that patient's predicted risk only slightly through this part, blood pressure and ST depression in an uneven way, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

ann_35.text: This part acts only on the 2 of 242 training patients whose thallium result is coded 4; 1 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 52-year-old woman with non-anginal chest pain and a thallium result coded 4), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 1% to about 5% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
Through it, a thallium result coded 4 raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 31% to about 79% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).

ann_36.text: This part acts on 50 of 242 training patients (21%); 22 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a resting blood pressure of 150 mm Hg, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and a normal thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 30% to about 41% (on the training data only).
Through it, older age raises the predicted risk only slightly and in an uneven way, and only once age rises above about 53 years (on the training data only).

ann_37.text: This part acts on 100 of 242 training patients (41%); 34 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 50-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, no chest pain on exercise, a maximum heart rate of 157 beats per minute and a normal thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 12% to about 19% (on the training data only).
Through it, maximum heart rate changes a typical patient's predicted risk only slightly, in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: Through this part, older age raises a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, and only while age stays below about 55 years: from about 4% at 42 to about 31% at 66 years, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure lowers it here in an uneven way, from about 31% at 110 to about 20% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).

For the typical patient it acts on (a 47-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, no chest pain on exercise and a maximum heart rate of 164 beats per minute), chest pain brought on by exercise raises the predicted risk from about 2% to about 8% (on the training data only).

Older age clearly raises the predicted risk in an uneven way, and even more so without chest pain on exercise (from about 6% to about 27%, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower, against about 36% to about 27% with it).

Higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk more, in an uneven way, for patients older than 56 years (from about 22% to about 28%), while for patients aged 56 or younger it goes from about 33% to about 3%.

ann_39.text: Through this part, older age raises a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, and only while age stays below about 55 years: from about 4% at 42 to about 31% at 66 years, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
Maximum heart rate, chest pain on exercise and sex change it only slightly through this part; by shape: maximum heart rate in an uneven way (on the training data only).
